title: Could AI for Lawyers Catch On Faster with In-House Attorneys?
author: Katya Fisher · Zach Abramowitz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source shifts from the cluster’s concern about reproducing expertise through deliberate apprenticeship to AI-enabled independent practice. Its speculative claim that graduates can self-teach and immediately produce high-quality work cuts against the cluster’s competence caution, while its stronger recommendation—targeting lawyers with 10–15 years of big-firm experience—implicitly relies on expertise acquired before using AI to operate independently.
qs: And I'm just going to start doing high-quality work today.
And ultimately, I think to me, the best target, if you can find them, is the lawyers who are 10 to 15 years in big law, and they're thinking, I'd love to leave, but how am I going to pull this off?

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: The source does not engage the cluster’s principal business-wide coordination and contract-intelligence proposition. It instead redirects the priority toward practitioner workflow efficiency, arguing that AI interfaces and clause extraction are counterproductive when they add interaction or duplicate document review. This complements the cluster’s usability concerns but advances a narrower lawyer-centred framing.
qs: I'm looking for a tool that's going to make me more efficient, not one where I have to spend the time that I would have spent redlining.
It's not helpful, at least not for me, and not for any lawyer I've ever worked with.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source shifts attention away from preserving law-firm apprenticeship and partner-succession routes toward AI-enabled independent practice. It speculates that AI could lower entry barriers for new graduates and, more plausibly, help experienced Big Law lawyers establish lower-cost practices, without addressing how foundational expertise, verification or succession would be maintained.
qs: So you know what's interesting is because I think, given your story and your background, I have actually thought that there's a huge opportunity today for someone coming right out of school to say, hey, listen, I'm going to buy some license to one of these AIs.
I think at that moment, if they can start using AI, they can provide very similar services to what they've been providing up until now, but at much less of a cost.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI can enable organisational redesign rather than merely assist incumbent lawyers. It extends the synthesis by proposing AI-enabled independent practices—especially boutiques founded by experienced BigLaw lawyers—as another delivery model capable of offering standard legal services at lower cost. However, this remains a hypothetical opportunity rather than evidence of realised performance or scale.
qs: And ultimately, I think to me, the best target, if you can find them, is the lawyers who are 10 to 15 years in big law, and they're thinking, I'd love to leave, but how am I going to pull this off?
I think at that moment, if they can start using AI, they can provide very similar services to what they've been providing up until now, but at much less of a cost.

st.t: Startup scaling: Founder context can become bottleneck
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core delegation proposition and adds a concrete mechanism: intensive training, system-building and clear escalation norms let a leader stop handling routine work while remaining available for senior guidance. Its evidence is personal in-house experience rather than comparative proof about legal-AI startups.
qs: You invest in the training stage so that you can then really delegate that to that person and they feel empowered.
And when to come to me and when not to come to me.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts that AI can complement lawyers while changing existing staffing and business models, and extends the proposition with a concrete forecast: experienced Big Law lawyers could use AI to launch lower-cost independent practices for standard transactions. This is a prospective, anecdotal delivery model rather than evidence of realised savings, demand or employment effects.
qs: And ultimately, I think to me, the best target, if you can find them, is the lawyers who are 10 to 15 years in big law, and they're thinking, I'd love to leave, but how am I going to pull this off?
I think at that moment, if they can start using AI, they can provide very similar services to what they've been providing up until now, but at much less of a cost.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI should be selectively deployed within lawyer-controlled workflows rather than treated as generally competent or wholly substitutive. It materially extends that proposition with a concrete in-house transactional design: specialised document ingestion, source-linked verification, familiar drafting integration and automation of bounded junior work, while retaining lawyers and firms for work beyond current capabilities. Its efficiency and savings evidence is experiential and vendor-reported rather than independently validated.
qs: So you can always verify and make sure that the tool is not hallucinating or making a mistake or overlooking something.
And there's a lot of deal work that at this stage cannot be automated.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s conditional, capability-specific framing: it reports useful targeted AI assistance and contract markup today while distinguishing these uses from complex, iterative deal negotiation that still requires humans. Its broader automation outlook is aspirational rather than evidence that autonomous workflows are currently reliable.
qs: I use it sometimes for more complex deals, to be fair.

But a lot of times, like when we're running really complicated PE deals, and there's a ton of lawyers on either side emailing each other 500 times a day, that's not something that's ready to be well automated yet.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that buyer-side incentives will drive selective automation of costly, slow junior work, pressure leveraged delivery economics and enable lower-cost independent practices, while substantial deal work and outside-counsel judgment remain indispensable. Its claims are anecdotal and speculative, consistent with the cluster’s caution that market-wide effects remain unproven.
qs: But paying a bunch of 28-year-olds, second-year, first-year associates to just read pieces of paper and tell me what they say, that needs to be automated.
And there's a lot of deal work that at this stage cannot be automated.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that specialised AI may let investment-focused legal teams insource routine due diligence and reduce particular law-firm instructions, while expressly preserving outside counsel’s role in deal work that cannot currently be automated. Its claims are conditional and experience-based rather than evidence of broad adoption or universal outside-counsel decline.
qs: These are the companies that I think, because they outsource so much work to law firms, if they begin using a software like yours and sending less work to law firms, in particular, the kind of work that law firms do, deals, investments, that could be like a real threat and sort of change the way, you know, due diligence is done.
And there's a lot of deal work that at this stage cannot be automated.

st.t: Legal leadership: Business capability complements legal expertise
st.an: The source supports the proposition by presenting broad generalist experience as valuable preparation for chief legal officer work and by advocating coordinated use of specialist outside firms rather than complete insourcing. Its evidence is personal experience and professional judgment, and it does not materially address operational systems or people management.
qs: It was when I went to big law and then subsequently when I became a chief legal officer, that suddenly I realized like, wow, my background, my experience makes me so powerful.
And I'll tell you when they're doing their job and when they aren't and what you need to do and how to be more efficient.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by arguing that practical legal document workflows require specialised software tailored to in-house needs rather than generic LLM use. It also confines automation mainly to routine document-reading work and acknowledges that substantial deal work still requires lawyers. Its support is experiential and anecdotal, without comparative performance evidence or a developed account of verification.
qs: And I found all of these challenges that I realized, you know, are sort of impediments and the reason why we needed to build something specialized.
And there's a lot of deal work that at this stage cannot be automated.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI will selectively automate routine legal production and reallocate some outside-counsel work without eliminating lawyers. It specifically targets junior document review while treating experienced partners, associate teams and non-routine deal work as indispensable; its lower-cost independent-practice and buyer-side claims are prospective and anecdotal rather than measured evidence.
qs: But paying a bunch of 28-year-olds, second-year, first-year associates to just read pieces of paper and tell me what they say, that needs to be automated.
And there's a lot of deal work that at this stage cannot be automated.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: Fisher supports the cluster’s distinction between targeted AI assistance and autonomous workflow replacement: she reports value in focused deal support while stating that complex negotiations are not yet ready for reliable automation. Her evidence does not address the broader concentration or durable vendor-value forecasts.

But a lot of times, like when we're running really complicated PE deals, and there's a ton of lawyers on either side emailing each other 500 times a day, that's not something that's ready to be well automated yet.

kp.k: Investment-firm legal departments could drive insourcing
kp.d: Abramowitz frames investment funds, private equity groups and family offices as an attractive market for specialised AI because they purchase substantial outside legal services. He predicts that adoption could bring diligence in-house and threaten law-firm deal work, rather than presenting comparative adoption rates or an established market-wide trend.
qs: Meanwhile, there are a ton of family offices, investment funds, PE funds, that send a lot of work to outside council every year.
I could very easily see if your product starts gaining traction that, no, now this process gets managed in-house. It doesn't get outsourced to a law firm.

kp.k: Fisher reports replacing outsourced diligence with internal AI
kp.d: Fisher says her team representing Constructure Capital had not outsourced diligence in a year, describing the process as 80% AI while retaining external counsel for negotiation and closing. She reports hundreds of thousands of dollars saved in the last year. These are the product founder's accounts of her own team's use, not independently documented results or a representative sample.
qs: We have not done a single due diligence in a year that we have it outsourced to external council.
External council, yes for the negotiation process, right? Closing the deal, all of that, but all the duty is done by us. It's 80% AI.
So I would say in terms of cost savings for us in the last year, and we've saved hundreds and hundreds of thousands of dollars just on that.

kp.k: Document-reading automation targets junior work and turnaround costs
kp.d: Fisher argues that paying junior associates to read documents and report their contents is unnecessary. Her illustrative board-appointment query involved about a thousand pages, a one-week wait, a two-paragraph answer and a $20,000 bill; she says she can now perform that work in 10 minutes. She also describes herself as 10 times faster as a lawyer, without supplying a systematic productivity measurement.
qs: But paying a bunch of 28-year-olds, second-year, first-year associates to just read pieces of paper and tell me what they say, that needs to be automated.
it would be about a thousand pages and send it out to a big law firm and wait one week and get an e-mail response, that's two paragraphs telling us exactly just what the answer is.
Not really advice, but just like this is what the documents say, and get a bill for $20,000.
I can do that stuff in 10 minutes now.
Now, I'm 10 times faster as a lawyer.

kp.k: Complex negotiation still requires outside lawyers
kp.d: Fisher distinguishes information extraction and company-status review from valuable outside legal advice. She regards some partners and associates as indispensable and says complex private equity negotiations, deal parameters and deal documents still require humans. Her qualification is explicitly time-dependent: she considers negotiation a possible future automation target, but not adequately automated at present.
qs: And there's a lot of deal work that at this stage cannot be automated.
Negotiation, negotiation for sure.
All the back and forth negotiation that goes on between lawyers at this stage of the game with AI, and this may be different in a few years, by the way, because it's moving fast, you need humans.

But a lot of times, like when we're running really complicated PE deals, and there's a ton of lawyers on either side emailing each other 500 times a day, that's not something that's ready to be well automated yet.

kp.k: Business users need document intelligence alongside lawyers
kp.d: Fisher says investment partners and fund CFOs need direct access to the same transaction documents as lawyers. Abramowitz interprets the product as serving the whole investment business, not merely its legal department. Fisher locates its value in extracting accurate business information rather than case-law research, reflecting her business-law practice rather than all legal work.
qs: partners and funds and CFOs and funds, they need to be as on top of these types of docs as the lawyers.
I don't remember the last time I like researched case law.
What matters to me is getting core information and looking at things the way somebody in my legal team would, right? And getting that accuracy.

kp.k: Specialisation addresses messy documents and inconsistent summaries
kp.d: Fisher attributes the need for specialised legal software to difficulties reading large, imperfect document collections and general-purpose models' inconsistent, prompt-dependent summaries. She describes building OCR capability and a prompt-free first summary covering main points, red flags and issues, followed by user questions. These are her technical and product claims, not reported comparative benchmark findings.
qs: The first is OCR, just the ability for a software tool to read the documents.
Try uploading a thousand pages of handwritten notes, photographs of a scan, you know, poorly scanned copies where the copy is like this, all of this sort of thing.
The next thing is that LLMs are not trained to know what to look for.
We've trained it that first of all, the first time you do a look, it's a one-click summary, there is no prompting.
These are what the docs are. These are the main points. These are the red flags. These are the issues. These are the things you want to take a look at, right?

kp.k: Human verification remains central to AI-assisted diligence
kp.d: Fisher describes full-document display and clickable source highlights as necessary for lawyers to check AI output, preserve agency and identify mistakes or hallucinations. Abramowitz separately reports hearing that M&A insurers ask whether lawyers actually verified clauses rather than relying on extraction. The model is assistance with human checking, not direct reliance on autonomous output.
qs: We still want to be able to check. We still want to have agency.
And so every single piece of information that Aracor gives back, you can click, you can get a highlight, you can see exactly where you got the information from.
So you can always verify and make sure that the tool is not hallucinating or making a mistake or overlooking something.

And they say that when they do underwriting calls for M&A insurance, which is a, you know, it's really prevalent, especially in private deals in the US, that one of the biggest questions they always ask is they say, in the course of your diligence law firm, did you verify all of these clauses or did you just rely on a technology to extract them?

kp.k: Workflow fit matters more than elaborate interfaces
kp.d: Fisher argues that tools should reduce work within familiar professional workflows rather than replace redlining with numerous interface operations or provide extracted clauses that still require separate document review. She describes her own continued use and her legal team's product involvement as design inputs, while recognising that the interface differs from more visually elaborate AI products.
qs: I'm looking for a tool that's going to make me more efficient, not one where I have to spend the time that I would have spent redlining. I now have to like press 70,000 buttons, right?
I have to go look at the document now. It's not helpful, at least not for me, and not for any lawyer I've ever worked with.
That's also why it's good that I have my legal team because we're really running product.

kp.k: Diligence extends to portfolio monitoring and transaction comparisons
kp.d: Fisher describes bulk review of employment and investment agreements to generate charts, flag missing IP assignments or unusual restrictions, and compare negotiated terms. She also reports comparing closing documents against term sheets and obtaining English information from foreign-language deal documents. Abramowitz emphasises that these uses continue after acquisition, rather than ending at transaction completion.
qs: These three people, they didn't sign IP assignment agreements. These two people have special restrictive covenants that you might want to take a look at.
I can throw like 100 safes in, get a quick chart and instantly see like what were the outliers, what were the anomalies, what were the standards, what did we do?
And I just throw it into Aracor with the term sheet and I'm like, does this match the term sheet?
And even if I'm using external counsel in Turkey, in Germany, right, I can still get all the information for myself in English and understand what's going on.

kp.k: Retained contract data could support organisation-specific standards
kp.d: Fisher describes a markup tool available both in the platform and through a Microsoft Word plugin that saves copies back to the platform. She links data retention to developing organisation-specific standards and future recommendations based on previous negotiations. The discussion combines currently described storage and comparison capabilities with prospective functionality, including suggestions to reuse terms from similar prior deals.
qs: The markup tool is inside the platform and it's a Microsoft Word plugin. And if you use the plugin, it will still save a copy in the platform, right?

So the idea is, you know, over time, the software is getting better and better and better because when you want to do red flags, when you want to understand is this standard, is this deal standard, we can create our own standard.
Because over time, like I said, the software is going to be able to say, hey, you're negotiating this deal. Last year, you did a deal just like this. Do you want to use the same terms?

kp.k: Multilingual markup can reduce routine external-counsel dependence
kp.d: Fisher says international operations involve side-by-side bilingual contracts and that previously she hired outside lawyers speaking the relevant language even for minor salary or job-title changes. She claims her markup tool can work across both languages, reducing that routine workload; the transcript supplies no measured accuracy or savings specifically for this feature.
qs: we have a lot of side-by-side dual language contracts, employment agreements, things like that.
And I used to always have to hire outside council that spoke these other languages even to do like two little changes, you know, to change the salary. It's a job title.
So the thing is that we can instantly go through both, and it makes things a million times faster and more efficient.

kp.k: Privacy and model flexibility shape international deployment
kp.d: Fisher describes a model-agnostic architecture, an Aracor small language model built off Llama, and private deployment for cautious organisations. She presents these as responses to changing model technology, GDPR-related privacy concerns and emerging regulation such as the EU AI Act, without establishing legal compliance. She also reports an unnamed state-government pilot successfully processing 250 pages of handwritten consumer complaints, a capability anecdote rather than a formal evaluation.
qs: So we do use large language models on the back end, but we're completely agnostic.
And we have built our own small language model, the Aracor SLM.

So if you want to be a product that people can use in an international setting, which I believe is quite ubiquitous these days, like we work in a very globalized economy, you need to be prepared for that as well. And for dealing with all the regulations that are coming down the pipeline, the EU AI Act, for example, et cetera, et cetera.
And they sent me 250 pages worth of consumer complaints scribbled. No problem. Our tool can do it with the SLM.
We can deploy our product privately.
Yeah, so we built off of Llama.

kp.k: Training and delegation provide a system-building analogy
kp.d: Fisher applies Ray Dalio's system-building principle to legal-team management: intensive training allows delegation and frees senior capacity. Abramowitz analogises that investment to training software, and Fisher agrees. This is a management account and analogy for AI-enabled scaling, not evidence of changes in staffing ratios or formal promotion structures.
qs: Ray Dalio talks in his book about how you need to build systems that you can walk away from.
I spent a lot of time training them.

I try to show them how to do things, how to be organized, how to think, to the point where I build systems and then I don't really have to do that much anymore, and then I can go on to the next thing.
You essentially spent a ton of time training your software now. And now it's like you've created the Ray Dalio concept, another system that you can walk away from.

kp.k: Hands-on AI adoption complicates seniority-based displacement narratives
kp.d: Fisher qualifies claims that AI will eliminate juniors and leave only seniors by pointing to senior decision-makers who discuss AI without using it and enthusiastic younger lawyers. Her support is observational, including a conversation with a senior lawyer aspiring to advise on AI despite little use, rather than workforce or adoption survey evidence.
qs: Everyone's talking about how like, all this AI tools are going to get rid of junior people, junior associates, all that's going to be left for the seniors. Yes and no
there's a lot of very senior people, lawyers and others who love to talk about AI these days, but they don't use it.
When you go talk to a bunch of 27-year-old recent law grads, they're on fire with this stuff.

kp.k: AI could enable lower-cost independent legal practices
kp.d: Abramowitz speculates that new graduates could combine AI tools and self-directed learning to start practices, and that lawyers with 10 to 15 years in BigLaw could use AI to offer similar services independently at lower cost. He limits his example to relatively standard deals rather than the largest transactions. These are proposed opportunities, not demonstrated practice outcomes.
qs: I have actually thought that there's a huge opportunity today for someone coming right out of school to say, hey, listen, I'm going to buy some license to one of these AIs.
the best target, if you can find them, is the lawyers who are 10 to 15 years in big law
if they can start using AI, they can provide very similar services to what they've been providing up until now, but at much less of a cost.
not for the biggest deals in the world, but for like, hey, this is a fairly standard deal.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Katya Fisher claims that specialised AI substantially accelerates in-house transactional work, brings document-based due diligence in-house, and reduces outside-counsel spending, while leaving complex negotiation to humans for now.
pts.d: Fisher reports being ten times faster as a lawyer using Aracor. She says her team has stopped outsourcing due diligence for Constructure Capital over the preceding year, with AI doing approximately 80% of that work, while outside counsel still handles negotiation and closing. She contrasts a historical document-information request costing $20,000 and taking a week with obtaining the information in ten minutes, and reports hundreds of thousands of dollars in annual savings. These claims concern reviewing documents and extracting information rather than replacing all legal advice. She also claims that AI can rapidly compare employment and investment agreements, identify anomalies and missing IP assignments, check closing documents against term sheets, explain foreign-language deal documents in English, and assist bilingual contract amendments and redlining. She anticipates further client-specific assistance using stored deal history to identify standards and suggest previously negotiated terms. Her account stresses specialised document reading, prompt-free initial summaries, and source-linked verification rather than reliance on generic LLM summaries. She qualifies junior-displacement narratives by arguing that some senior decision-makers do not use AI while recent graduates are enthusiastic users. The interview does not establish a comparative in-house-versus-law-firm adoption rate; the host's forecasts about easier sales, new solo firms and market disruption are not treated here as Fisher's claims.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of Fisher's first-hand use of her own company's product, transactional examples, internal testing, and practitioner experience; no independent performance study or itemised savings analysis is supplied.
pts.d: Fisher speaks as both Aracor's CEO/co-founder and an active chief legal officer. She grounds the efficiency and insourcing claims in her own legal team's work for Constructure Capital and describes specific workflows: a roughly thousand-page shareholder-document query, employment-agreement review, comparison of investment instruments, term-sheet checks, multilingual M&A work, and live simplification and redlining of a clause during negotiations. The transcript provides self-reported timings and savings but no transaction counts, controlled comparisons, accuracy rates, calculation methods or independent corroboration. Her claims about general-purpose tools' limitations rest on repeated testing and discussions with engineers, without naming tested model versions or presenting results. She invokes experienced co-founders and advisers and unnamed prominent fund users as support for relevance beyond her personal workflow. A pilot involving 250 pages of handwritten consumer complaints supports her claim of document-reading capability, but no measured error rate is given. Her observation about senior practitioners' limited AI use includes a single anecdote about an unnamed senior lawyer. Statements of superior quality and future-proofing are product claims rather than independently demonstrated findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Fisher presents core efficiency gains as already achieved by the January 2025 interview, while treating automated complex negotiation and richer historical-data assistance as future possibilities.
pts.d: The conversation identifies its recording date as January 2 and the document dates the episode to 2025. Fisher's preceding-year insourcing and savings claims therefore refer approximately to 2024. She presents the due-diligence, markup, small-language-model and private-deployment capabilities as currently functional, with immediate trials available. The scope is business and investment legal work, not criminal practice or every legal task. She explicitly retains humans for back-and-forth negotiation in complicated private-equity deals and says that could change in a few years, without giving a definite prediction or deadline. Standard NDAs, SaaS agreements and employment contracts are stronger current markup use cases than complex deal negotiations. Future client-specific standards and deal-term suggestions depend on retaining and reusing a client's accumulated documents. Reliability is conditioned on handling imperfect scans and large document collections, providing legally relevant summaries, and enabling human verification against full source documents. International use additionally requires attention to privacy and regulatory constraints; she presents model flexibility and private deployment as ways to address these needs.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries in Fisher's account are investment-focused in-house legal teams and their business colleagues; the directly exposed provider work is junior-heavy outside-counsel document review rather than all law-firm services.
pts.d: In-house lawyers at venture-capital and private-equity businesses gain faster access to deal information, reduced external expenditure, and greater ability to review documents internally. Fund partners and CFOs can also use document information directly because they need to understand the same agreements as lawyers. International legal teams gain English-language visibility into foreign-language transactions and assistance with dual-language contracts, potentially reducing reliance on external counsel for minor amendments. Large law firms, their junior associates, and partners earning revenue from routine document review face reduced demand for that work in Fisher's account. She nevertheless describes certain outside partners and associate teams as indispensable and retains them for negotiation, deal documentation and closing. Practising lawyers remain responsible for checking outputs: the product is framed as making an attorney more efficient, not eliminating professional agency. Recent graduates may have a practical adoption advantage over senior gatekeepers who discuss AI without using it; Fisher does not quantify any resulting employment change. Privacy-sensitive organisations and international users are additional intended beneficiaries of private deployment. The government-office pilot extends the claimed document-reading capability beyond investment practice, but the interview does not make a broader access-to-justice claim.
